text: The orchestra was playing the Romanian “Doina.” More accurately, only Ancheto was playing, with a flute solo, while the others accompanied. We were listening from the inner lounge. But, you might ask, who are these “we”? Who indeed? It is well known who: the Senator, Othello, Stuvencho, and I. Before us stood a long bottle of white Chateau Sandrovo and another of Giesshuebler. Carelessly settled around the table, with cigarettes in our mouths, we caught the fiorituras of “Doina” and had surrendered ourselves to a pleasant *far niente*. Tomorrow is Sunday—there is no work, we can stay a bit later. The music is decent, the waitresses are pretty, we—somewhat overripe bachelors. Perfect!

We were just sitting there when, at one point, the flute grated on my ear with a few false notes, and at the same time, the whole orchestra went out of tune. At that very moment, Stuvencho burst out laughing and cried: "That damn Othello! What a joker! Just look at him!..." The Senator and I turned around at once, and what did we see! That devil Othello! Where does he get these antics from? He had stood up without us noticing, asked for a slice of lemon, and after catching the flute-player's eye with some gestures without the others seeing, he started to tease her, making her mouth water with the lemon juice. Well, naturally, she’s a young girl, she craved something sour, her mouth filled with saliva, her lips puckered—try playing the flute after that! Laughter...

The music stopped. From the street, the shout of a kid was heard: “Ne-w news-pa-pers Na-tion-al Great-ness!” What National Greatness? As if! Infected with laughter from the comedy with the lemon, we burst out laughing again. At that moment, Gedros also arrived.
— Oh, Gedros, hi! Sit down! Do you want some wine?
— Oh, Othello, hello, hello, little bird. Go on, wipe your little nose — the eternally cheerful Gedros said tenderly.
— Gedros, what is this newspaper they were just shouting about in the street?
— What! Is it possible you don't know about Bay Ganyo Balkanski's newspaper?
— Fool!
— I am telling you seriously. Ganyo Balkanski, editor-proprietor of the newspaper "National Greatness." Ah, it is quite a story. Don't you know?
— Are you serious?
— Seriously, brother. Wait, let me tell you. Today they told me this story in detail and I will tell it to you as if I had been there.
We gave orders to close the door of the inner salon and Gedros began. Here is what he told us:

At Bay Ganyo’s, a meeting was convened. Gathered were: the host himself, Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Danko Harsizina, and they were deliberating—what sort of enterprise to seize upon, so as to take the most profitable advantage of the situation.

— We ought to get a bite of something too — says Bay Ganyo, — patriotism just like that, high and dry — is all nonsense. Now tell me, as things stand, from where can the best profit be struck? You, Gochoolu, what do you say?
— Me? To tell you the truth, Bay Ganyo, I still hold to my idea: let's open a Russian tavern.
— What?!
— Let's open a Russian tavern — Gochoolu replies seriously and decisively.
"— Well, what about you—how? Have you sided with Mother Russia again?" Bay Ganyo wondered.
— But come, let's get this straight, it's not about Mother Russia here, the thing is — which way the wind blows...
— Where? In your head?

— In Bulgaria. A fool is he who does not take advantage. Now is the time — a tavern. I have roamed through Muscovy, I’ve picked up a thing or two. A tavern with two sections — for the gentry and for the peasants.
— But where will you find muzhiks in our country! — Bay Ganyo asked in bewilderment.
— Well, at last, are we all nobles then, Bay Ganyo?
— Fine, what next?
— Further on: we'll treat him to some music, an organ—you must have seen one, Bai Ganyo?
— If I don't see it, who will? — Mr. Balkanski replies haughtily.

— You're right. An organ and, of course, tea. We'll round up a dozen kids, but let them not be dark-eyed, let them look like little Russians; we'll pull some boots on them, a red shirt each, then we'll give them Cossack haircuts — there's a whole tavern for you! We'll bring in Russian newspapers, vodka, snacks, then slap a sign on top — "Russian Tavern" — and you're all set. Eh?
— I do not approve! — cried Dochoolu solemnly. — I do not approve! If it is a matter of snatching a profit from the wind that has blown, then it would be best to open a kvass factory...
— We hit the jackpot! — laughed Danko the Rogue. — Do you want to open a bakery?
— No, brother—I’m talking about Russian kvass. It’s a sort of thing... like this here, call it pear cider, call it boza...
— A fine business! We're going to become boza-sellers now — the Scoundrel took offense.

— No, brother, it’s not about the drink—the name is what matters; just say: "Russian kvass!"—they’ll be falling over themselves to get there. Haven't you heard what the French are doing now? They’ve struck it rich, money—no joke!
— Nonsense. I don't want kvass — declared a dissatisfied Danko.
— Well, what do you want? — Dochoolu asked him angrily. — Come on, tell us so we can see?
"Let's start a bank!" blurted out Danko the Scoundrel.
— You are a fool!
— Why?
— Put the quarrels aside — Bay Ganyo intervenes.
— Why should I be a fool! — Danko continues, enraged, and shoots murderous looks at Dochoolu.
— Well, shut up now, sit down. Tell me, what do you have to say about the bank.
— But let him say, my dear fellow, why should I be a fool?

— He’s going to found a bank for me! This thing isn't popara to be slurped up — growls Dochoolu under his mustache, unsettled by the looks and the threatening tone of Danko. — Is this popara? It's a bank!
— It is popara, after all! — roars the Scoundrel.
— What do you mean, popara? Why on earth should it be popara? — snapped Dochoolu.
— Shut up, you people. Is this why we’ve gathered? — Bay Ganyo calms them down. — Dochoolu, sit in your place.
— But why on earth should it be popara?

One word led to another and the matter escalated; Danko the Thief, as you know him, is quick to pick a fight, and Dochoolu doesn't hold back either — they would have killed each other, until finally Bay Ganyo, [intervening] here and there — calmed them down.

Danko sits down in his place and begins to lay out his plan for the founding of a bank. “The business is easy—we’ll issue five to ten million in shares, we’ll collect the cash, lend to this one, lend to that one, with good interest of course, to merchants, to municipalities, and if the government finds itself in a tight spot—a million or two for them as well. Why! We’ll have them write up a charter, half the profit for us, half for the shareholders. Besides—we’ll keep some shares for ourselves, whether we put in money or not. You, Bai Ganyo, are an influential man, you’ll clear your throat at two or three gateways and it’s done!”
"— This business is not a spoonful for your mouth; there are more capable people than you, let them hatch it, and then we’ll stick our beaks in," Bay Ganyo states patronizingly.
Gochoolu and Dochoolu nod their heads approvingly.

— Wait, let me tell you now what I have in mind — Bay Ganyo shouts authoritatively and stands up. — Do you know with what? We won’t prosper with a tavern, nor will we set up a bank properly, and as for your Russian kvass, Dochoolu, that’s a completely trivial matter; so, shall I tell you what?
Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Harsizina have been turned into all ears and impatience.
— Shall I tell you what? Eh?
— Well, say it then, stop being silent — Danko utters nervously.
— Shh! The hasty bitch gives birth to blind pups. Shall I tell you? Eh? Gentlemen! Let's publish a newspaper! — blurted out Bai Ganyo, and a look of triumph dawned on his face.

If some sea monster had slipped into our interlocutors' room at that moment, it could hardly have increased the staggering impression produced by Bay Ganyo’s last words. In the first minute, they were as if petrified; in the next, Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Danko Harsizina began to glance at one another very timidly, as if asking: “Has Bay Ganyo, God forbid, lost a screw?” One could neither laugh nor pity him. He would boil over. Finally Gochoolu, fear or no fear, decided to hint at it from a distance:
— Your Grace, Bay Ganyo, you like, every now and then—he-he, if you'll excuse me, I mean to say, you like... well... the jokes, so my point is, he-he...
— What?
— No, Bay Ganyo, I only said it to... sort of... But look, your honor, about the newspaper... are you serious?

— What do you mean "seriously"? How else? Of course, seriously! Is it such a great knack to publish a newspaper? Just cast all shame aside (though there’s no need for that), and then curse left and right. That’s how!
— Well, if it is to be so, I agree — declares Danko Harshizina.

— Exactly, of course! We’ll call Gunya the Lawyer; he’s a master of editorials, and we—some reports, some short notices, some telegrams. Since the goal is to smear this one or that one—it doesn't take much philosophy to do that. Danko, run down to the office, please, and call Gunya the Lawyer here.

— Do you see that brigand? — said Bay Ganyo after Danko Harsazina left. — When it comes to swearing — leave it to him! He'll curse you so that your kidney will sting. He makes a total mockery of a man. And whether it be right or wrong, he doesn't even blink. A formidable rascal!

It cannot be said that Gochoolu and Dochoolu were delighted by these qualities of Danko Harsizina; nor can it be said that in their conception of journalism Danko appeared to be a suitable editor. Within them, memories were still preserved of another time, of the Turkish era, when the printed word might have muddied the waters for them, but did not erupt with such a lava of hellish insults and curses. But the storm of wild passions, raging over a whole series of years, the demoralizing influence of the demoralized press, the coarse, all-consuming materialism, and the possibility of easy enrichment by lulling the conscience following the example of the ruling elements—all these phenomena have covered their purer feelings with such a thick layer that an entire, no less long-lived and essentially new epoch is needed to excavate this layer of abominations until those buried pure feelings emerge like remnants of past greatness.

And now, when Bay Ganyo explains his plan to them for the publication of a newspaper, its direction, and the individuals who will take part—Gochoolu and Dochoolu feel a certain pang in a remote corner of their hearts; they sense that there is something crooked in this business, something that should not be; but upon the heavy layer that presses those pure feelings to the bottom, Bay Ganyo adds a new layer and suffocates them. Eloquently, with enthusiasm, with passion, he lays out the material benefits that will be gained from their enterprise. And no more convincing arguments are needed for Gochoolu and Dochoolu.
The door opens and Gunyo the Lawyer appears on the threshold with his sharp fox-like snout, followed by Danko the Thief.
— Gunyo, what do you say? — Bai Ganyo turns in a friendly manner. — We want to publish a newspaper, eh?
— Why not, let's publish. Is there any easy money? — asked Gunyo with a wink and a quick movement of his fingers.
— You just enjoy yourself.
— But is there any?
— There is, there is, just enjoy yourself.
— Fine. What kind of newspaper should we publish — for the government or the opposition? Tell me quickly, because customers are waiting for me.
— Now that's the trick — whether government or opposition? I don't know, damn it, how long the current ones will last.
— Tell me quickly, customers are waiting for me.
— Do you know what, Gunyo? — mused Bay Ganyo, without paying attention to the lawyer's words. — I think for the time being we should go along with the government...
— Quite so, quite so, it's best with the government — Gochoolu and Dochoolu hasten to declare.
Bay Ganyo looks at them angrily for interrupting him and continues: — ...And then, once we sense that their legs are shaking, we give them a kick and get back into power with the new ones, eh?
— Fine. Did they promise you a little something?
— It is known, it cannot be without it.

— Since that’s how it is, let’s begin — Gunyo the Lawyer decides, and here a conversation starts about the way they will publish the newspaper, and about a kind of direction that their organ will follow on certain issues. A decision is made to comply with the times and the circumstances, and even with the profit, if "the Lord has willed it." For Russia, "we’ll let out a bit of: our liberator, the brotherly Russian people, long live the Tsar Liberator (God rest his soul), but otherwise, when we find ourselves in a tight spot, we’ll go back to the old 'Trans-Danubian Governorate.' Regarding Macedonia, we’ll keep a bit quiet, you know, it doesn’t quite fit, the times aren’t helping. Austria this, that and the other, Triple Alliance — it doesn’t suit at all..."
— But what about the youth, what are we going to do with the youth? — Gochoolu speaks up. — They’ve started to stir, too!
"We'll lead them on, what can you do, troublesome youngsters, sometimes you'll even tip your hat to them, such times have come, there's nothing to be done," says Bay Ganyo with a sigh.
"— Nothing to be done, is that it?!" growls Danko the Rogue, and his eyes darken. "Damned unpruned stick! Let me just get my hands on them, and then..."
— Stand still, Danko...
— D... d-d-dust and ashes...
— Leave them now, don't! Sit in your place. There is time.
— Hurry up, Bay Ganyo, for clients are waiting for me — Gunyo the Lawyer calls out impatiently.

— Listen here, Gunyo, you know what... (come on, forget about those damn clients of yours!)... you know what? You sit down tonight and write an editorial. Give it such a display of loyalty that the Prince himself will be stunned. Put in there: Your humble children, Our father and sire, in the dust of Your August feet—string them along like prayer beads, you know how. And mention a word or two about the people, as is proper. Do you understand me? Good. And then give the opposition a good roasting. Say there: Those traitors, those...
— "Traitors" is outdated now, let's put "scoundrels" — Gunyo corrects.

— Alright, put "scoundrels." And don't forget to put "the fatal one for the Bulgarian people" as well. Devil take it, I like that word "fatal" very much! When I say it like that, f-f... f... fatal, it’s as if I’m f-f-f-grabbing someone by the throat... I like it awfully much!
— And as for me, what I like best is when I give someone a good cussing out," blurted out Danko the Scoundrel candidly, "it lightens my soul I don't know how!"

— Well done, you rascal, long may you live! — exclaims Bay Ganyo, delighted, and pats Danko on the shoulder. — The deal is done. You, Gunyo, will write the editorial, as I said, right? And you, Gochoolu, and you, Dochoolu, cook up some reports, some telegrams.
— But what telegrams, what reports? — the two asked in bewilderment.

— What kind? All kinds. Don’t you see the other newspapers? Write there: Your Royal Highness, the people rejoice on bended knees and unanimously pray to the Almighty... and so forth; stuff in there whatever comes to your mind. Say there: The Bulgarian people have given thousands of proofs that when their rights are touched, every single one of them rises to their feet... and... such-and-such... with tears in their eyes... and so on. Finally, why scribble so much; curse the opposition, and that’s that. Indeed! Why should we sit down now and get mushy with various philosophies. And who will understand you! Isn’t the point to pull the wool over their eyes—keep the wagon rolling. Isn’t it so?
"Well, goodbye then, for I have clients waiting," mumbled Gunyo the Lawyer and took his hat.
— The devils are waiting for you... Anyway. Well, goodbye. And listen, Gunyo, have the editorial ready early tomorrow. Best of health!
Gunyo heads towards the door. After him, Gochoolu and Dochoolu stand up, to whom Bay Ganyo gives the necessary instructions.
— Listen here, gentlemen, we've forgotten the most important thing — Bay Ganyo shouted after them — how are we going to name our newspaper?
— Well said, Bay Ganyo, but we are... like that! — responded Gochoolu and Dochoolu.

— "This is a serious matter," says Gunyo the Lawyer, "and do you know why it is serious? Because those devils took all the good names, they didn't leave any for us. But some will still be found. I think it is most fitting to name our newspaper 'Justice,' and we'll add in parentheses a 'fin de siècle'." (Author's note - end of the century, Fr.)
— What?
— It is a French word, you do not understand it.
— We don't want French; if you can, put in some Latin, just for the sake of custom.
— Shall we give it a "Tempora mutantur"?...
— Go ahead, if it’s appropriate. You, Gochoolu, what is your opinion? — Bay Ganyo turns.
— "Justice" is a nice word, but it seems to me that "People's Wisdom" will be even nicer — Gochoolu answers.
— I don't agree — Dochoolu spoke up — that name looks too much like a priest's; it's better to call it "Bulgarian Pride."
— And you, Harsaz, what will you say?
— Me? How should I know? Let's just slap together a "People's Courage," and let whatever happens, happen. We'll put Sari-Chizmeli Mehmed-aga as the responsible editor, eh?
— It’s all nonsense. Shall I tell you? — Bay Ganyo declares authoritatively. — We will name our newspaper either “Bulgaria for Us” or “National Grandeur.” Choose one of the two.
— “People’s Greatness”! Agreed! “People’s Greatness”! That’s it, that’s it, long live!
— Well, goodbye, Bay Ganyo.
— Goodbye.
Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Gunyo Advokatina exit.
"You, Danko, stay; you and I will write short articles."

— All right. Order them to bring mastic and meze now and let’s get to work. And don’t let them drag in that sour okra again; see to it that there’s some decent meze—a newspaper is to be written here, it’s no joke.

They brought mastic and meze. But Old Man Manolcho will ask, what kind of meze? That is not important; what is important is that Bay Ganyo and Danko the Thief rolled up their sleeves to lead public opinion.
— Danko, man, our neighbor is really putting on airs with me, acting like he’s so educated, so honest, and I don’t know what other nonsense. Should we give him a piece of our mind?
— Not only that, we'll level it with the ground — declares the expert in profanity.

And the writing begins... "We learn that..." — writes Bay Ganyo, and sets out upon a sheet of white paper such black slanders against his neighbor, of which not only had he never "learned" at any time, but which had never even crossed his mind in his dreams.

Bay Ganyo writes, he writes and crosses out; he is constantly dissatisfied with the venom of his arrows: "thief" is a mild word to him, he crosses it out and writes "brigand," but that word has become commonplace, so Bay Ganyo adds "broad-daylight" and joins it with a "fatal." The neighbor, his wife, his children, his kin — under Bay Ganyo's pen, they emerge as phenomenal monsters... He reads his work to Danko Harsizina. Danko, his eyes shining from the mastika, enthusiastically encourages the master of the entrefilets.
— Drive, drive, drive! Ram them, damn it, don't stop for anything, for nothing! Raaaam! — thunders Danko Harsizina, as if he were commanding an artillery battle...
— There, gentlemen, is how Bai Ganyo’s organ was founded — Gedros concludes his story.
We reopened the door to the inner salon and the orchestra thundered the wonderful march from Wagner's "Tannhäuser".
Farewell, indulgent reader! You will encounter in this little book some cynical words and scenes, I could not avoid them; if you can depict Bay Ganyo without cynicisms — be my guest!

Farewell to you too, Bay Ganyo! God is my witness that I have always been inspired by good feelings while describing your stories. Neither a sense of malicious condemnation, nor contempt, nor frivolous laughter has guided my pen. I too am a child of my time, and certain individual events may have involuntarily diverted me from strict objectivity, but I strove to reproduce the essence of the sad reality. Your brothers, I believe, are not as you are depicted, Bay Ganyo, but for now they are in the background; they are only now beginning to assert their existence, whereas you—you are present, your spirit flies and encompasses the entire social order and leaves its mark on politics, on parties, and on the press. I harbor a faith within me that a day will come when you, after reading this little book, will reflect, sigh, and say: We are Europeans, but not quite there yet!...
Farewell, it would be no wonder if we meet again.
Sofia, 17 March 1895.
